column11: | RT-1 | **A `hwbp.py` run left the game wedged after detach — 0.02 s of CPU across 3 s wall, 99 threads alive.** The run itself succeeded (control 171 hits, target 9+9), and the wedge was only noticed because three key presses aimed at the front-end did nothing and a screenshot showed the game still on the Square Enix splash a minute later. `hwbp.py` clears the debug registers in a `finally` and calls `DebugActiveProcessStop` with an unchecked pre-attach `DebugSetProcessKillOnExit(FALSE)` (protection was not verified; [EXP-017](../_experiments/EXP-017-debugger-exit-policy.md) later corrects and tests that setup) — but it clears them across `threads_of(pid)` **enumerated at detach time**, so a thread created during the run could keep a programmed DR7 and take debug traps with no debugger attached. **That is a hypothesis, not a finding**; the correlation is one run. This matters beyond one experiment: **a runtime instrument that leaves the target unusable makes every later observation in the same session worthless**, and nothing currently checks the target is still running afterwards. Related: an earlier session recorded a *different* wedge — during the run, fixed by restricting context writes to the trapping thread. **CORRECTED 2026-09-08, the same day it was filed: the hypothesis is wrong.** Three controlled runs — attach-only (`--no-arm`, 21.4 % of a core), armed on a settled game (39.1 %), and armed during the boot sequence with 123 threads (34.4 %) — all left the game **alive**, against a no-attach baseline of 23.4 %. `hwbp.py` is exonerated for this configuration and the stale-DR7 mechanism is unsupported. **The wedge itself was real** (0.02 s across 3 s wall) and its cause is **unknown**; the block that observed it also ran `window_focus.py` and `runtime_input_probe.py` three times in between, and **none of those was tested**. Liveness is now measured by `process_liveness.py` as a rate rather than judged. **UPDATED 2026-09-08 — it is STATE-DEPENDENT, and the withdrawal above was drawn from the wrong state.** Three pre-load runs are clean; **two in-world runs both wedged the game and it never recovered** — one open-ended with a per-frame control (hwbp's own liveness check reported `FROZEN`, 0 hits on everything), one tightly bounded at 60 hits in 0.2 s wall (still 1.6 % and falling afterwards). **So hit rate is not the mechanism**, and neither is thread count (101 in-world vs 105 and 123 pre-load). The practical constraint on goal 3: **a capture from a loaded save costs the session that save**, which the ~2-minute reload recipe in §4bk makes affordable but which must be planned for. | OPEN |

Both total 0x54. WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A HARMLESS ALIAS. (1) The two records DISAGREE ABOUT READINESS, IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS: the flat type is TYPE RESOLVED at type level while 20 of its 21 field rows sit at SEMANTICALLY IDENTIFIED; the chain's field rows are TYPE RESOLVED while its leaf type PClusterHeader is SIGNATURE RESOLVED. So 'what rung is the cluster header on' has two answers depending on which row a reader opens. (2) Any census that counts fields or types across the store DOUBLE-COUNTS these 21 fields and counts one structure as two (or four) types - which inflates category 22, the largest type population in the database. (3) A reconstruction reading both gets two names for one struct and no statement that they are the same. NEITHER IS WRONG AS A VIEW: the chain reflects the engine's actual C++ hierarchy and carries the RTTI names, the flat row is a database-side flattening that is easier to read. The defect is having both with NO STATED RELATIONSHIP between them. NOT RESOLVED UNILATERALLY: choosing which survives - or making the flat row an explicit alias of the chain - is a store-convention decision, and it is the same schema owner as the union question already routed in OPUS-REQ-SWE2-STRUCT-THE-TYPE-STORE-CANNOT-DECLARE-A-UNION. Routed there rather than deleting a row. BOUND: this compares the two records' declared offsets and names; it does not re-derive either from the image, so if one of them is wrong about a field the other may be the correct one and the duplication is still real. column7: The scripted-camera page stated that one shake evaluation takes sixteen words from the gameplay MT stream 'once per frame for every driver whose state is non-zero', which with four drivers reads as a frame-wide ceiling of 64 draws; and a static census of 98 call sites over 66 functions was available to be read as evidence that one consumer dominates the stream by volume.
column8: UPHELD FOR ASTRA 2026-09-20 (OPUS), and verified independently before accepting. The caller 00314370 is 85 bytes with SHA-256 3213b13bf8c8acae8fea9773e24cde1bea29a4b29c5f0d3a756f740a4c41252a, matching ASTRA's citation exactly, and its body is a FIVE-SLOT LOOP: xor ebx,ebx at 00314381; call 00263FF0 for the slot record; test byte [rax+0x10],1 as the per-slot guard; calls to 003DA050 and 003DCFB0 on the eligible path; inc ebx; cmp ebx,5; jl back to 00314383. THE FOUR-DRIVER LOOP IS NESTED INSIDE THIS, so the ceiling per invocation is up to 20 driver visits and 320 words rather than four drivers and 64, and it is CONDITIONAL on the bank, state and entry guards rather than fixed. Separately, 'per frame' was never established: 00314370 is reached from several sites, so invocations per frame is an unmeasured scheduling fact. A per-slot conditional quantity was being reported as a frame-wide bound. ON THE SECOND POINT ASTRA IS ALSO RIGHT: a static call-site census counts WHERE a generator is called from and is not a measurement of HOW OFTEN, so it cannot support a dominance-by-volume claim; only a run distinguishes those. WHAT SURVIVES: the sixteen words per evaluation, the sampler being the gameplay MT's consumer through 0037D1F0, a finished driver at state 2 continuing to draw because the sampler only exits early on an entry of -1, and the conclusion that camera shake is not cosmetic for stream reproduction. The RATE is withdrawn; the MECHANISM stands. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE QUEUE: ASTRA's proposed live sampling plan is still worth running, but it must scope occupancy PER OWNER SLOT and publish invocation counts, because a one-slot snapshot would systematically undercount shared RNG activity - which is the point ASTRA filed.

Filed by OPUS on 2026-09-20 as OPUS-CONTRA-KEEPIMAGE-VS-SCRATCH2-COORDINATES and recorded only in the OPUS inbox, not in this ledger.
column8: PROMOTED TO THE LEDGER AND THE PREMISE IS NOW EXECUTED, 2026-09-20 (OPUS), adopting SWE2-ORACLE's EXP-138 (sealed and committed at c36dcda20: 449/449 functional, 384/384 mutants, stable x3, 21 bodies executed with site-exact fault parity). EXP-138 ran both accessors and reports EF640 returning 0x2164280 and EF2B0 returning EF640()+0x200 = 0x2164480. I re-read both bodies against the shipped image before adopting: 002EF640 is EIGHT bytes, `lea rax,[rip+0x1e74c39]` resolving to 02164280 followed by `ret`; 002EF2B0 is TWENTY bytes, `sub rsp,0x28` / `call 002EF640` / `add rax,0x200` / `add rsp,0x28` / `ret`. Both agree with EXP-138 exactly. SO THE 0x200 OFFSET IS NO LONGER A STATIC READING - it is isolated original-code execution, and the coordinate-frame hazard behind the original error is confirmed rather than merely argued. WHY THIS IS WORTH A ROW RATHER THAN A NOTE: the error it describes is silent. Rows measured in the buffer frame LOOK correct at the payload offsets they land on, and nothing in a field census catches a uniform 0x200 shift - only comparing the two accessors does. Any future measurement that reaches this data through 002EF2B0 must state which accessor it used. The offending rows were stripped before publication and none entered the store. BOUND: this confirms the OFFSET and the two accessor bodies; it does not re-derive the original scratch measurement, which remains withdrawn rather than re-attributed.

column7: EXP-132 describes PATHW's round-failure target twice and the second description contradicts the first. The opening paragraph says QWALK(B->A, flag=1) != 1 returns 1 immediately, which is the fall-through to 0x33A40B; the third bullet then calls the SAME address a dead tail - 'jumps to the 0x33A40B dead tail (add [rax],al x2 then epilogue - faults on the small-int return; a full B->w->A path makes the round fail)'. Read that way, a round whose two rotated probes both come back unreachable ends in a fault rather than a return.
column8: THE ADDRESS IS A LIVE RETURN PATH, NOT A DEAD TAIL - corrected 2026-09-20 (OPUS) from the shipped image while adopting EXP-132. 0x33A40B is `b8 01 00 00 00` = `mov eax, 1`, followed at 0x33A410 by `e9 2f 01 00 00` = `jmp 0x33A544`, the function's own epilogue. It is PATHW's SHARED RETURN-1 EXIT and it has three predecessors, all of which I read: the direct-probe fall-through at 0x33A409 (`je 0x33A415` not taken), and the two round-failure branches `jne 0x33A40B` at 0x33A4B9 and 0x33A53C. Nothing faults on any of them. WHERE add [rax],al COMES FROM: decoding one byte late, at 0x33A40C, turns the `01 00` / `00 00` tail of the immediate into `add [rax],eax` / `add [rax],al`. This is an OFF-BY-ONE DISASSEMBLY START, the same class as the rip+displacement mis-adds EXP-132 itself logs as its scope correction 1 (BKSC took three tries) - an address arithmetic slip that yields a plausible-looking wrong answer rather than an error. WHAT IS AND IS NOT AFFECTED. The executed record is UNTOUCHED: under emulation 0x33A40B executes `mov eax,1; jmp`, so the 98/98 functional cases and 99/99 mutants measured the real behaviour and the 'blocked' and 'probe2-reached r1/r2' cases all returned 1 as the bytes require. THE PROSE IS WHAT IS WRONG, and it is worth a row because it inverts the one thing a consumer needs from PATHW: a round in which neither Q(B->w) nor Q(w->A) reports 1 makes the function RETURN 1, and only when both rotated rounds pass does it reach `xor eax,eax` at 0x33A542 and return 0. A reimplementation written from the bullet would raise, or treat the case as unreachable, exactly where the shipped function answers. EXP-132's first paragraph and its bullet's parenthetical intent are both correct; only the dead-tail characterisation is withdrawn.

column7: EXP-136's verified behaviour contract for MABESP (003588B0) names the handle's fields 'bank=(h>>0x14)&0x7FF, sel=(h>>0x10)&0xF' and then uses an undefined symbol 'gen' for the rest - 'gen>=d[T+0x20] -> 0 ... gen>=d[arr] -> 0; e = q[arr+8+gen*8]' - and EXP-136's own function table calls the body a 'bank/sel/gen handle decode'. The name 'gen' attaches the generation role to the field that indexes the pool, and 'bank' to the field that is compared for staleness.
column8: THE ROLES ARE THE OTHER WAY ROUND, AND THIS STORE ALREADY NAMED THEM - corrected 2026-09-20 (OPUS) while adopting EXP-136/137. I read all 143 bytes of 003588B0 from the image. The decode is `mov edi,ecx / shr edi,0x14 / and edi,0x7ff` (0x3588CB-0x3588D3), `mov eax,ecx / shr eax,0x10 / and eax,0xf` (0x3588C4-0x3588D9) and `movzx ebx, cx` (0x3588DC) - so the third field, which EXP-136 leaves undefined, is h & 0xFFFF. Then: ebx (the 16-bit field) is what bounds-checks against d[T+0x20] (0x3588FA) and d[pool] (0x358905) and what INDEXES the pool at `q[rcx+rbx*8+8]` (0x358909); edi (the 11-bit field) is what the entry is compared against at `movzx ecx, word [rax+0x16] / cmp ecx,edi / cmovne rax,0` (0x358913-0x358925). THE 16-BIT FIELD IS THE INDEX AND THE 11-BIT FIELD IS THE STALENESS TAG - the opposite of what 'gen' and 'bank' convey. The database had already named all three from the ENCODER side: 0046BE80 packs ((w[rec+0x16] & 0x7FF) << 4 | (b[rec+0x15] & 0xF)) << 16 | w[rec+0x00], which is ActorStorageRecord's handleTag11, handleTag4 and selfIndex; and 003588B0 is already named ActorHandle_ResolveRegistryEntryByPackedId. Encoder and decoder agree field for field, read independently. SO THE PACKED ACTOR HANDLE IS: bits 30-20 handleTag11 (staleness tag, cycles 1..0x7FF, period 2047, never 0), bits 19-16 the owning ActorManagerSlot index, bits 15-0 selfIndex; bit 31 unused. WHY THE NAMING MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING COSMETIC: it says which field a release must bump. Bumping the 16-bit field because it was called 'gen' would move the handle to a different record instead of invalidating it, and the 2047-period wrap the handleTag11 row already warns about would be silently lost. EXP-136's ARITHMETIC IS CORRECT AND IS ADOPTED UNCHANGED; only the three names are corrected, and the missing definition of the third field is supplied.

column7: The ActorStorageRecord +0x015 handleTag4 row credits two writers in its evidence cell: 'written 00266624 (initialiser) and 00239207; read by the handle encoder at 003589B9'.
column8: 00239207 IS NOT A WRITER OF THIS FIELD - it writes +0x15 of a DIFFERENT object. Corrected 2026-09-20 (OPUS), found by cross-reading the nav accessor experiments against this row and confirmed from the image. The host is 002391C0, 80 bytes. Its subject is not the record: it takes an object from 0031B760, then works entirely through `q[r8+0x6A0]` - `mov eax, dword [rcx] / test al,4 / and eax,0xFFFFFFEF / mov [rcx],eax` (0x2391DC-0x2391E5), `mov byte [rcx+0x15], 0` (0x2391EE), `or dword [rax],0x10` (0x2391FD) and finally `mov byte [rax+0x15], bl` (0x239207). THAT OBJECT CANNOT BE AN ActorStorageRecord: it is read and written as a 32-BIT BITFIELD AT +0x00 carrying bits 0x4 and 0x10, whereas this store has ActorStorageRecord +0x000 as `uint16 selfIndex` (the array index the record was fetched by), +0x002 as `actorIndexClass` and +0x004 as `hitObjectBindState`. A dword read-modify-write at +0 would be overwriting the record's own index with flag bits. It is also reached as `q[X+0x6A0]`, the immediate sibling of the `q[X+0x698]` sub-object pointer that EXP-135's LHELP dereferences, which is the shape of a small flags record hanging off a world object, not of the 0x288-scale actor record. NOT CLAIMED: what that object IS - only that it is not this type, so the offset match at +0x15 is a COLLISION, not a second writer. CONSEQUENCE, AND THE LIMIT OF IT. With 00239207 removed, 00266624 is the only writer this row still credits, and that is what lets the field's meaning be closed in the same package - see the handleTag4 row. IT IS NOT A PROOF THAT NO OTHER WRITER EXISTS, and this row should not be read as one. An image-wide census of byte-sized writes to [reg+0x15] run while filing this (all decodable extents; 148 failed to decode and are excluded) finds 58 SITES ACROSS ROUGHLY THIRTY HOSTS - 0025E4C0 alone writes the offset eleven times, and 002621D0, 002C6F70, 00333C80 and the 0036Axxx family all write it. +0x15 IS A CROWDED OFFSET, so membership here can only be decided by proving the receiver, never by matching the displacement. That is the general lesson this row exists to carry, and it is the same instrument error as the mis-attribution itself.

column7: The high-band family disposition recorded for DL-1 and on the widget message protocol page gives three properties as the reason 285, 287 and 289 are taken off the open-question count as a family rather than named one by one. The second is that all three are 'tested by a dedicated je on their own large constant BEFORE that receiver's ordinary small-id table', cited as 0055CD53 cmp eax,0x11D, 00280DF1 cmp eax,0x11F and 00569204 cmp eax,0x121.
column8: THERE IS NO DEDICATED PRE-TEST; THOSE ARE BINARY-SEARCH ROOTS - found 2026-09-20 (OPUS) while verifying FABLE's own withdrawal of the FIRST of the three properties, and read from the shipped image across all seven receivers. Each cited site is cmp / jg / je, the pivot of a comparison tree, not a special case ahead of a table: 0055CD40 is cmp eax,0x11D / jg 0x55DB1D / je 0x55D84B, and 00280DE0 (0x280DF1), 002C2320 (0x2C2592), 00565E00 (0x5661E3) and 005691E0 (0x569204) all have the same shape. Only 00557DB0 has a bare cmp/je. The large ids sit at the ROOT of the tree because they are the largest values it sorts on, which is the opposite of being handled outside it. AND THE SIXTH RECEIVER NEVER COMPARES ITS CONSTANT AT ALL. 003FF360 contains no 0x11D anywhere, yet it genuinely answers 285: its root is cmp ecx,0xC / jg 0x3FF784, and the high half runs sub ecx,0x12 / je (18) / sub ecx,1 / je (19) / cmp ecx,0x10A / je - THE SUBS ARE CUMULATIVE, so that last compare is against id-19 and 0x10A + 19 = 285. So a raw cmp-immediate scan misses this receiver for a reason INDEPENDENT of the foreign-id-space reason already recorded: the id is decremented before it is compared. The instrument fails in two ways, not one. THE THIRD PROPERTY SURVIVES and is corroborated by the same reading: the two 64-bit arguments at record +8 and +0x10 are real, and 003FF360 reads them at 0x3FF7AB (mov rax,[rdx+0x10]) and 0x3FF7B5 (cmp qword [rdx+8],1). CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DISPOSITION, WHICH IS FABLE'S TO MAKE: two of its three properties are now withdrawn - the first by FABLE (ids 285 and 287 have THREE receivers each, not one; verified independently here from widget-message-handlers.tsv) and the second here. The disposition's conclusion that these are 'one screen talking to itself' rested on the single-receiver reading in particular. NOT CLAIMED: that the family reading is wrong - only that two of the three stated reasons for it no longer hold. PROPAGATION NOTE: the withdrawn first property is carried in _index/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md DL-1, which FABLE's withdrawal scope named only the protocol page, so that index needs the same amendment; it is FABLE's file and is not edited here.

column7: The type store declares ActorWaitSlot (0x28, 04-Actor-Entity, SIGNATURE RESOLVED) and VmResultEntry (0x28, 01-Script-VM-Native-Bridge, TYPE RESOLVED, PROVEN) as two types, and each counts once in the store's 465-type population and once in every by-type census built from it.
column8: THEY ARE ONE ARRAY DESCRIBED TWICE, AND THE STORE ALREADY SAYS SO IN PROSE - found 2026-09-20 (OPUS) by crossing the route column against the ctype column. Both carry the BYTE-IDENTICAL route `CHAIN ActorStorageRecord +0xA8 stride=0x28 count=slotCountA8` and both are 0x28, and VmResultEntry's own instance column ends '- THE SAME ARRAY ActorWaitSlot DECLARES'. So this is not a collision discovered here; it is a known duplication that no instrument reports and no column resolves. THE TWO DESCRIPTIONS AGREE WHERE THEY OVERLAP, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THEM ONE TYPE RATHER THAN A DISPUTE: VmResultEntry names exactly two fields, +0x0C value (i32) and +0x15 commandPhase (u8), and ActorWaitSlot names the same two at the same offsets with the same types, plus nine more. VmResultEntry's other three rows are declared gaps totalling 35 of its 40 bytes. IT IS A STRICT SUBSET. AND THE RUNGS ARE INVERTED, WHICH IS THE PART THAT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: the 5-row view that describes 5 of 40 bytes is TYPE RESOLVED / PROVEN, while the 15-row view that names 11 fields is only SIGNATURE RESOLVED. A reader trusting the readiness column would take the weaker description as the better one. This is the 'size known is not TYPE RESOLVED' failure in its clearest form. WHAT IS NOT DECIDED HERE, DELIBERATELY. Which name survives is an OWNERSHIP question across two categories - 04-Actor-Entity and 01-Script-VM-Native-Bridge - and a merge would move field rows between owners, so it is routed rather than performed. The ActorStorageRecord +0xA8 ctype is left anonymous until it is settled, because writing either name there would silently pick the winner. INSTRUMENT GAP THAT LET THIS STAND: check_route_collisions.py populates only from routes with a LITERAL base/stride/count - 20 of them - so it is structurally blind to CHAIN and EMBED, which is where every parent-relative duplicate lives. It reports 'clean apart from the known duplicate' over a population that cannot contain this one. || CLOSED 2026-09-21 (OPUS): THE FIX IS APPLIED, verified in the store today. There is NO type row and NO field row named VmResultEntry; the only types.tsv line containing the string is ActorWaitSlot's own, which cites it in prose, and the four fields.tsv hits are ActorWaitSlot field descriptions naming the offset correspondence. ActorWaitSlot 0x28 survives as the single declaration, still carrying the route CHAIN ActorStorageRecord +0xA8 stride=0x28 count=slotCountA8 that made the duplication visible in the first place. check_type_refs reports 0 dangling references, so no field anywhere still names the retired type as its ctype. The double count this row warned about - one object contributing twice to the 465-type population and twice to type-debt-by-type.tsv - is gone with it.

column7: EXP-133's measured semantics for RDEC (0032A6E0) give the destination of its packed-vector store as '`cvtdq2ps` + `mulps [0x908E30]` (1/4096 fixed-point scale) -> `movdqu` scratch `0x23151B0`'. OPUS then answered REQ-OPUS-NAV-LOS-FINDINGS on 2026-09-20 saying that RDEC's sites had been re-read against the image and listing 'movdqu scratch to 0x23151B0' among the values that matched exactly.
column8: THE SCRATCH IS 0x22D91B0, AND BOTH THE EXPERIMENT AND MY OWN CONFIRMATION OF IT WERE WRONG - corrected 2026-09-20 (OPUS) from the raw bytes while building the corridor-query family's write census. The instruction at 0032A735 is `f3 0f 7f 15 73 ea fa 01`, a movdqu store with disp32 = 0x1FAEA73 and a length of 8, so the next instruction is at 0032A73D and the target is 0032A73D + 0x1FAEA73 = 0x22D91B0. The published figure is high by 0x3C000. MY OWN ERROR IS THE MORE INSTRUCTIVE HALF AND IS NOT SOFTENED HERE. I did disassemble RDEC and I did see the displacement; I then computed the sum IN MY HEAD, got 0x23151B0, found it equal to the number I was checking, and reported the row as verified. A confirmation that is arithmetic done by the checker, unshown, against a value the checker already has in front of it is not an independent check - it is the bias the check exists to defeat. The fix is mechanical and was adopted immediately: the family write census resolves rip-relative targets with the disassembler rather than by hand, which is what surfaced this. WHY IT IS A SILENT ERROR RATHER THAN A CRASH: 0x22D91B0 and 0x23151B0 are BOTH past raw section data, so both ship zero and neither can be told from the other by reading. A reimplementation that plants RDEC's scratch at the published address writes 0x3C000 bytes away from where the shipped body writes and faults nowhere. FIFTH OCCURRENCE of the rip+displacement class in this family's records - EXP-132 logged three mis-adds for BKSC as its own scope correction 1 and called that the fourth. BOUND: this corrects the destination ADDRESS only. RDEC's semantics are otherwise unaffected and stand as adopted - the root at 0x209A670, the 16-byte record stride, the 64-byte vertex stride via sx16(w[rec+2]), the three movsx lanes with a stale fourth at rsp+0x2C, the 1/4096 mulps constant at 0x908E30, and the atan2f into out+0x14 were each read from the image and each hold.

column7: The dtor cell of BootSingleton01F7F598 read '00189CE0 + 00189570 per game-application.md's boot table; not re-read here' - two addresses recorded as the singleton's destructors on the strength of a column in another page, with the row itself admitting they had not been read.
column8: BOTH ARE PER-FRAME UPDATE BODIES, NOT DESTRUCTORS - corrected 2026-09-20 (OPUS) while closing the lifetime column for the frontier categories, where these were 2 of only 2 unestablished dtor cells in 51 types. 0017D6E0 calls them back to back through the lazy getter: 'call 00189120 / mov rcx, rax / call 00189CE0' at 0017D769, then the identical fetch-then-call for 00189570 at 0017D776. game-application.md itself names 0017D6E0 'the per-frame subsystem pump' that 'fetches and advances 13 lazily-constructed singletons' (lines 231, 391, 463) and calls these two 'different update bodies' (line 514) - so the source page was right and the transcription into a DESTRUCTOR column was the error. Their behaviour confirms it independently: 00189570 gets four floats from 001ACC30 via out-parameters, tests the returned bool, and distributes them into the boot sub-blocks through 00185C30, which WRITES its target's +0xC8, +0xD0 and +0xD4 and then calls a virtual on it. A destructor does not write fields, and nothing is destroyed twice per tick. THE CELL IS NOW UNESTABLISHED, NOT NEGATIVE: no release path was found for this singleton, but no image-wide search for one was run either, and the difference is recorded rather than smoothed over. THE LESSON IS THE PROVENANCE, not the addresses: a cell that cites another page's table and says 'not re-read here' is carrying that page's COLUMN SEMANTICS as well as its values, and those do not travel. The admission in the cell was accurate and should have been treated as a blocker.

column7: ManagerSub0209AC30_00C0 carried the route 'PTR 0x0209AC30 +0xC0' and an evidence cell stating the creator stores the block 'with mov [rbx+0xC0], rax at 00293286, where rbx = *(0209AC30)'. The type NAME encodes the same one-hop path. _index/OPEN-QUESTIONS.md (line 1101) and _index/_inbox/repos-f1.md independently spell the same address as *(void**)0x0209AC30 + 0xC0.
column8: THE ROUTE WAS ONE HOP SHORT; THE TRUE SLOT IS *( *(0209AC30) + 0x2F8 ) + 0xC0 - corrected 2026-09-20 (OPUS). RBX IS REBOUND BETWEEN THE TWO INSTRUCTIONS THAT WERE READ: 00293191 does 'mov rbx, [0209AC30]', but 002931CD then does 'mov rbx, [rbx+0x2F8]', and it is that second value the store at 00293286 uses. The load was read, the store was read, and the reassignment between them was not - so the object named as the parent is the parent's PARENT. FOUR THINGS AGREE ON THE CORRECTION. The creator 00293170 walks 0209AC30 -> +0x2F8 -> +0xC0 and stores there. The releaser 00292B10, found in the same pass, walks the identical chain, frees [owner+0xC0], frees the owner, and nulls the slot. The creator GUARDS on the middle hop at 002931AE ('cmp qword [rbx+0x2F8], rax' with rax zero), which a one-hop reading leaves unexplained. And 16-UI/Shop-Screens/the-shop-screens.md line 351 already wrote the chain out in full - '[0209AC30] -> +0x2F8 -> +0xC0 -> dword[+0x40] & 1'. The store held the right answer on one page and the wrong one in the type row. THE OTHER TWO PAGES ARE NOT WRONG, which is the subtle part and the reason this is filed rather than silently fixed. *(0209AC30) + 0xC0 IS a real, live, usually non-null pointer: 00280120 is a 20-byte predicate reading exactly it ('mov rcx, [0209AC30] / cmp qword [rcx+0xC0], rax / sete al'), and OPEN-QUESTIONS calls what it finds 'the menu object'. Those pages describe THAT field correctly. There are simply TWO different +0xC0 pointers one hop apart, and the type row attached its description of one to the address of the other. WHY IT MATTERED: the old route was not merely imprecise, it was RESOLVABLE AND WRONG. A generator following it would not fault - it would silently return a different live object. A wrong route that faults is a bug; a wrong route that returns is a trap. SAME CROWDED-OFFSET LESSON AS CON-132: +0xC0 is not a distinctive displacement, and only the base register's provenance separates the two objects that have one. So the declared byte layout is the true one and SWE2-STRUCT's strided attribution does not hold at this offset. The instruction is real; the arithmetic is inert. NOT CLAIMED: the addend is not provably zero for sums of magnitude below ~1e-3, which a combined radius is not; and why the group is loaded as four floats when the fourth slot holds flags is a question for the owner of 003DA6A0, not a layout question.

column8: OVERLAY -- NEITHER READING IS WITHDRAWN, because both are evidenced and they are not reconcilable by picking one. THE FLOAT SIDE: 003DA6A0 is called at 002E468F as (rcx=rdi+0x50, rdx=rdi, r8=rbx+0x50, r9=rbx) and does 'addss xmm6, dword ptr [rbp+0xC]' and 'addss xmm0, dword ptr [rsi+0xC]' - it ADDS the fourth component of each 16-byte field AS A FLOAT into a running sum. That is arithmetic, not a copy: two flag bytes and a padding word summed as a float would be garbage. AND THE RECEIVER IS CORROBORATED INDEPENDENTLY OF THE ROUTE STRING: immediately after the call, 002E4694 does 'mov rax, qword ptr [rdi + 0xf0]' and then reads a float at [rax+0x20], and MovementContext declares +0x00F0 as steeringCursor, a pointer. So rdi is a MovementContext on this path by the type's own declared layout, not merely by the artifact's attribution. THE BYTE SIDE: three sites read or write +0x5C as a single byte through two different routes - 0025BEC7 'cmp byte ptr [rbx+0x5c], 0' and 0025C87C 'movzx eax, byte ptr [rsi+0x5c]' via ctxarg1, and 0026647C 'mov byte ptr [rsi+0x5c], 1' via actorarg:rdx+0xB8. A byte written as 1 and compared against 0 is a flag, and that is equally not a float. SO THE FINDING IS AN OVERLAY, not a mis-carve: the same four bytes are summed as a vector W component on the steering path and used as flag bytes on the actor path. WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: which is the declared type of the storage and which is the reinterpretation, whether the two paths are ever live at once, and whether the vector sum simply tolerates whatever is there because its result is discarded on that arm. A union needs a discriminator and none was found. || NARROWED 2026-09-21 (OPUS), NOT CLOSED - the union still has no discriminator and this row stays OPEN. What IS now settled is the residue this row itself named: 'whether the vector sum simply tolerates whatever is there because its result is discarded on that arm'. IT IS NOT DISCARDED - it is the return value. 003DA6A0 read whole (112 B): it calls 003DA730 then 003A1D30 twice, saving the first result in xmm6, then does 'addss xmm6, [rbp+0xC]' (003DA6E8) and 'addss xmm0, [rsi+0xC]' (003DA6ED), then 'addss xmm0, xmm6' (003DA701) and RETURNS xmm0. AND THE SHAPE IS NOT A VECTOR'S W LANE: the callee loads a SCALAR at [base+0xC] with addss; the 16-byte framing comes from the caller passing rdi+0x50 as the base. Its companions say what the scalar is for - 003DA730 reads [rcx+8] and scales it by -1.0 (01CEBC9C = BF800000) and differences [r8] against [rdx], an x/z lateral term that skips y, and 003A1D30 is 23 bytes of cvtss2sd / andps 7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF / cvtpd2ps tail-jumping 00861F14 - an ABSOLUTE VALUE. So the expression is |lateral_1| + a[+0xC] + |lateral_2| + b[+0xC]: two absolute distances plus a scalar from each object, which is a clearance or half-extent term and not padding. WHY THIS RAISES THE STAKES RATHER THAN SETTLING THEM: the float lane is no longer a plausible don't-care W component that a flag byte could squat in harmlessly - it carries a value the result depends on. A reconstruction that stores 1 into +0x5C as a flag corrupts that addend, and one that keeps it float loses a flag three sites read and write. BOTH readings remain evidenced and the discriminator - whether the two paths are ever live on the same object at the same time - is still not found. That is the question to answer, and it is a LIVE one: it needs the two paths observed on one object, not more static reading.

column8: THEY ARE TWO DIFFERENT TYPES OF TWO DIFFERENT SIZES WITH TWO DIFFERENT ROLES. Read 2026-09-21 (OPUS). THE SIZES ARE ALLOCATION IMMEDIATES: 0018B4AB is 'lea ecx, [rbx + 0x30]' into malloc for the object stored at 01F7F5E0, and 0018C9F9 is 'mov ecx, 0x20' for the one stored at 01F7F5E8. The 0x30 object's constructor 0018AD00 writes four fields the 0x20 object has no room for - classMask at +0x20 (0xFFFFFFFF, 0018AD39), forwardSplit at +0x24, a zeroed word at +0x29 and reverseMark at +0x2C (-1) - and reserves 5,000 entries through 0018B320 at 0018AD48, which the 0x20 object never does. THE ROLES DIFFER AND ONLY ONE OWNS. 0018B810 walks the 0x20 list at 01F7F5E8 and calls every element's slot 0 with edx = 1, the scalar-deleting form, so free runs (0018B850-0018B860); 0018B040, the 0x30 list's clear, calls 0018B3F0(list, 0), whose shrink arm at 0018B43B-0018B46B only moves pEnd back to pBegin and touches no object. AND THE TEARDOWN ORDER FOLLOWS: at both sites the non-owning list is cleared first and the owner destroys second - 0017CD53 then 0017CD60 in the frame tick, 00188204 then 00188211 at the end of the render pass. WHY THIS IS EASY TO GET WRONG AND EXPENSIVE TO GET WRONG: the globals are 8 bytes apart in .data, both objects open with the same three-pointer EASTL vector triple and both constructors pass the same discarded 'EASTL vector' string, so they look like the same type - but a reconstruction that gives either list ownership of the objects double-frees or leaks one command object per enqueue per frame. column8: THE ALLOCATOR WRITES A WORD AT +0x26, INSIDE THAT DECLARED DWORD. Found 2026-09-21 (OPUS) while reading the allocator the store already cites for the +0x20 clear. In one function, on one record: 002E25EC is `inc dword ptr [rdx + 0x24]` - the WHOLE DWORD incremented - and twelve instructions later 002E2613 is `mov word ptr [rdx + 0x26], r8w` with r8d zeroed at 002E25EF, so the UPPER HALF is cleared after the increment. A word store at +0x26 either names a second field or is a partial write of the declared one, and the field map currently allows neither reading. WHAT THE STORE'S OWN NOTES SUGGEST, and it is only a suggestion: slotIndex at +0x1A is described as 'the low half of the packed handle' and generationStamp as 'the packed handle's high half'. A 32-bit handle built from a 16-bit slot index and a 16-bit generation would make +0x24 a u16 and +0x26 a separate u16, and the dword `inc` a cheap increment whose carry into the high half is then wiped - which would explain why the clear exists at all. I HAVE NOT MADE THAT CHANGE, deliberately: splitting a declared uint32 into two u16s on the strength of one write, without a census of what READS +0x24, is exactly the 'a field name does not prove semantics' failure. A reader that loads the full dword would refute it. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: a reader census over NameBindingEntry +0x24 - if every read is 16-bit the split is right; if any read is 32-bit then +0x26 is a partial write of one counter and the clear is a wrap, which is a different and equally recordable fact. RELATED AND NOT RESOLVED BY THIS: +0x22 remains a genuine 2-byte gap, untouched by this allocator, and it is the single cheapest piece of type debt in the store - 2 bytes, and the only debt in its whole category. || RESOLVED 2026-09-21 (OPUS) THE SAME HOUR, AND AGAINST MY OWN HYPOTHESIS - the uint32 declaration is RIGHT and the split I floated would have been wrong. A reader census over the 51 functions this type's field rows cite, disassembled in full: FIVE READS OF +0x24 AND ALL FIVE ARE 32-BIT - 002E939D 'mov eax, dword ptr [rcx+0x24]', 002E97E8 'mov edx, dword ptr [rax+0x24]', and 002EC72A / 002EC73A / 002EC773 all 'mov eax, dword ptr [...+0x24]'. A 16-bit field would have produced 16-bit reads and it did not. SO +0x26 IS A PARTIAL WRITE OF THE DECLARED DWORD, NOT A SECOND FIELD, and the mechanism is now readable: increment the whole counter, then zero its upper half, which CAPS THE GENERATION AT 16 BITS BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by any explicit wrap or mask. AND THE IDIOM IS DELIBERATE, because it appears TWICE in two different functions on the same record - 002E25EC with 002E2613 in the allocator, and 002E944B with 002E944E inside 002E9360. A one-off could be a compiler artefact; a repeated pair is the author's intent. WHAT THIS ADDS TO THE STORE is not a correction but the WHY behind an existing note: the field row already said generationStamp is 'the packed handle's high half' beside a 16-bit slotIndex, and this is the code that keeps it inside 16 bits. The field row's evidence is extended with it; no declaration changes. THE LESSON I WANT RECORDED: I filed this as a width contradiction on one write and explicitly refused to act on it without a reader census - and the census refuted the reading the write suggested. The refusal was the right call and the census cost ten minutes. NOT RESOLVED BY THIS: +0x22 is still a genuine 2-byte gap and still the cheapest single piece of type debt in the store.

column8: THE GRAPHICS INSTANCE'S +0x9C0 IS NOT THIS TYPE'S FIELD; IT IS ITS CONSUMER'S CURSOR, AND IT IS EIGHT BYTES. Measured 2026-09-22 (OPUS) over every rip-relative operand in the image at each cell, with the widths taken from the operands. (1) WIDTH AND KIND DIFFER: the gameplay cursor 02EB4230 has 8 accesses, ALL 4-BYTE, in four bodies - 00863BF0, 00863C80, 00866B90, 00866D60 - while the graphics cell 01F7FFC0 has 4 accesses, ALL 8-BYTE, in one body, and that body walks it as a POINTER: `mov rax, qword ptr [01F7FFC0]` / `mov ecx, [rax]` / `add rax, 4` / `mov [01F7FFC0], rax` at 00194855-00194862. An 8-byte field at +0x9C0 would span +0x9C0..+0x9C7 and cross this type's declared extent of 0x9C4, so it cannot be the declared uint32. (2) NEITHER GRAPHICS GENERATOR ROUTINE TOUCHES IT: 0018EE20 (the twist) has no operand at or above +0x9A0 at all, and 0018D740 (the seeder) has exactly one, `lea rdx, [rcx + 0x9bc]` at 0018D761, which is the array's end sentinel and not a cursor store. The gameplay instance is the opposite case - its own seeder's final store puts the cursor at 02EB4230, which is why the field is real there. (3) THERE IS A THIRD CELL, UNDECLARED: 01F7FFC8 = +0x9C8 has 6 accesses, all 4-byte, all in 001946E0, and it gates the twist - `mov eax, [01F7FFC8]` / `test eax, eax` / `jne` skips `lea rcx, [01F7F600]` + `call 0018EE20`, then `dec eax` / `mov [01F7FFC8], eax`. It is a remaining-count kept by the consumer, not by the generator. (4) 01F7FFC4 HAS ZERO ACCESSES, which the type row already noted - and the reason is now visible: it is the upper half of the consumer's 8-byte pointer, not empty space. SO THE RESOLUTION IS THE ROW'S OWN PRINCIPLE, APPLIED ONCE MORE. That row already excludes the gameplay lazy-init byte at 02EB4234 on the ground that "a field that exists for one instance of a type and not the other is not a field of the type; it is a guard the gameplay CALLER keeps next to its own instance". The same is true above the array for the graphics instance: 01F7FFC0 and 01F7FFC8 are the noise-texture builder's cursor and refill count, kept next to the stream it draws from. The shared layout is the 624-dword core; `index` at +0x9C0 is real for the GAMEPLAY instance, where its generator writes it, and absent for the GRAPHICS instance, where no generator routine touches it. NOT CHANGED BY THIS: the declared extent 0x9C4 and the `index` row both stand - they describe the gameplay instance correctly. What was wrong is the sentence attributing 01F7FFC0 to this type, and it is corrected in the instance cell rather than by re-extending a type on the strength of one consumer's bookkeeping.
